Field notes · No. 4

Two weeks stuck, and a book that said that’s fine

DJ, founderOctober 14, 20262 min read

This fall I spent two weeks stuck on one screen. The very first one you see when you open Nook. Should it ask you to pick a folder before anything else, or just let you start? I rewrote it four times. Every version felt wrong in a new way.

Around then I was rereading Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance. I keep a board for every book I actually finish, and this one started the usual way. I pasted the Goodreads link, the cover came in, and I drew a region called Highlights.

Then one line stopped me. Pirsig, on the moment you can’t see the next step:

Stuckness shouldn’t be avoided. It’s the psychic predecessor of all real understanding.

Robert M. Pirsig, Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance (1974)

I typed my own note right next to it: “Two weeks stuck on the first screen. Maybe this is the predecessor part.” I drew an arrow from his sentence to mine and labeled it “That’s me.”

That arrow is the whole reason I keep reading boards. A highlight on its own is a nice sentence. A highlight with an arrow to your actual week is advice you gave yourself, using someone smarter’s words.

It helped, too. Not with an answer, with permission. I stopped trying to force a fifth version and spent two days just watching people open the app. The fix came out of that and turned out much simpler than any of the four drafts: two buttons, “Get Started” and “Open Workspace…”, side by side.

The book board is still there. Every few months I open it and find that a different highlight has an arrow on it now.

If you read with a pen, try this once. Paste the book and draw one arrow from it to your own life. The arrow is the part you’ll come back for.
